utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor against Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The record should note that the Court is fully constituted for the legal argument which follows. There are two issues with which we have to deal. The first relates to the expert evidence of Dr. Schrader and the second to some affidavits which the Defence have produced. We will begin with the argument in relation to Dr. Schrader. We have before us, first of all, his report. Secondly, the document setting out the Prosecution's objections and application to rule the report inadmissible, and finally, we have a reply by the Defence. Now, having had the objections and reply in written form, is there anything that anybody wants to add to what's in these documents? Mr. Nice, you've seen the Defence reply is there anything you want to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence reply, which is one of three documents recently served in a form and with a style that I find personally unhelpful and, where it intends to be, offensive, needs to be dissected to some degree in order that one can see what, if any, substance there is in the argument being advanced and what is, in reality, likely too obscure. And if one looks at the first paragraph of the opposition to our motion, line five reflects an attempt by the Defence to set this argument in a different and entirely false context describing John Elford as a quasi-expert, a phrase already deprecated in this Tribunal, and not reflecting the fact that the Tribunal who heard all these had accepted his evidence which was of an entirely different nature and partially entirely responsive to the Chamber's request but, in any event, an exercise built on the analysis of documentation about true dispositions. And so this is not a question of, as it were, pitching Schrader against Jonathan Elford and indeed a moment's consideration of the Schrader report shows how different it is in every conceivable way from the material provided by Mr. Elford. If one goes to the next paragraph, we find as much as can be found in this document to justify calling, as a witness, somebody who is, it appears, a historian, a military historian to do the Chamber's job for it. It's sought to be established, line three of the second paragraph, that he has performed a meticulous study of the testimony and documents for the purpose of explaining the military significance of facts that might not be apparent to a layman. The phrase "military significance" is not itself further explored, and it does not respond at all to the proposition that we made clear. Namely, that there is no identification in the document of the expertise relied upon or how that expertise can react upon source material to provide an useful form of evidence for the Chamber. The curriculum vitae is set out, and indeed we'd already set it out in the sense of a summary way, and nothing there is of particular relevance. The very high point can be found on the next page, page three of the document right in the middle of the page, where, in an unquantified and unqualified way, he has apparently taught military history and strategy, but not being quite clear whether it's historical strategy or current strategy, and that's all that's said about it. It's also said, at the foot of the second paragraph, that he has extensive military qualifications in a variety of military specialities and in the following paragraph has published in a number of areas related to military strategy and military tactics. The Chamber will, in due course, if it wishes to contrast that with the entirely specific Balkan -- substantially Balkan based expertise of Dr. Cigar. The fourth page contains the distracting terminology with second line in and continues to inject, and I just observe that the suggestion that the use of documentation in the Defence case is in some way wrong or improper again obscures the reality. The Prosecution case here has been built, not only on contemporaneous accounts, for they are the valuable accounts, but on contemporaneous documents that support those accounts and all too frequently confound Defence witnesses. It then says in the middle of this paragraph five lines down, "The Prosecution called numerous experts or quasi-experts of its own, including virtually every one of the numerous military witnesses." I don't challenge, of course, that from time to time and in a sensible and permissive approach taken by these Chambers, witnesses of all kinds may speak from some limited expertise, but there is no question that this has been quasi-experts or anything of that sort. What it is, then, that Dr. Schrader's report given that there is no association of expertise in conclusion, what is it that it does? The next paragraph reveals it, line three, "He presents an overview," that's the Chamber's job. He's providing a view. We then see that at page five, they attempt to deal with the criticisms we make to which they respond by saying that the testimony from the Blaskic case will be introduced as transcript evidence. By no means is that necessarily the case, it hasn't even been advanced that such transcript will be sought to be introduced. And then we return to a relevant phrase, dribs and drabs. The witnesses identified in paragraph eight of its papers will be witnesses whose transcripts we'll seek to introduce. It categorises in the next paragraph, quite improperly and without any support, Dr. Cigar as a spy. It's not the position at all. Spies gather intelligence. Dr. Cigar is a person whose has expertise and training to work on material of all kinds, much of it open-source material, and to draw from it particular conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally in the "Conclusion" paragraph, we return again to, as the Chamber will see and I don't seek to dignify it by reading it out, the sort of terminology in lines 3 and 4 that they regard as helpful to their case. Now, if one, at random effectively, for that's all I did this morning, opens the Schrader report -- I chose initially page 40 and I'll just go through a couple of pages -- one can see, and this is beyond what I've already drawn to your attention in our motion, I think I highlighted here footnote 179, a reference to the United States Joint Chiefs of Staff publication, which defines "active defence". Now, this is rather interesting, because not only is this document of Dr. Schrader's, which is very substantial and must have been in preparation for a very long time, not only has it relied extensively on very recent Defence evidence that has been given which has either been incorporated or was forecast, but we see here, interestingly, given the witness who's currently under cross-examination, a particular term of art, "active defence", which this non-military witness who is just before us has sought to use as a term of interpretation, having no military experience. That's a tiny point, but it just occurred to show what may be going on here. If we then go on to page -- and again examples only -- 42, footnote 193, we see this: "Some details of the events in Busovaca in January 1993 are derived from an interview by the author with Ante Juric, former commander of the 1st Battalion of the Zrinjski Brigade." It's not available to us, not suggested that it's going to be available to us at all. Let's look at the following page, page 43. The last paragraph, this comment about one of the witnesses who has been before the Chamber: "With a typical rush to judgement, Lieutenant Colonel Stewart misread the situation, opining that --" it makes reference to his diary. That's not a judgement for an expert. That is entirely a judgement for the Court. So that is exactly the sort of observation that you find throughout this document. If you go, for example, to page 46, it's another reference to -- and these are all just what I turned up this morning in addition to those that I've already cited in our document -- page 46, another reference and summary from Colonel Stewart. "He testified he didn't expect the outbreak of a major conflict in the Lasva Valley. However, the HVO authorities, having been caught flat-footed by the probing attack of the ABiH in January, were not surprised. The targeting of the ABiH for intelligence purposes began soon after the 20/21st January attacks, and on the 25th of March, Zeko, the intelligence officer of HQ OZCB, issued an intelligence estimate." This is all built, as we now see, on footnote 214, a document not yet produced, and, of course as we're going to know from elsewhere, evidence of Zeko in the Blaskic case. This is -- and one can go on until one reaches the entirely extravagant conclusions which I think I did draw to your attention; for example, at page 53 about Ahmici. He asserts the facts are unclear, as are the interpretations; portrayed as an unprovoked massacre. "The best explanation seems that a justifiable HVO spoiling attack on Muslim forces went out of control." It asserts that it was a legitimate military target. All matters for the Trial Chamber. And then I think I already made reference in the -- perhaps it's worth having a look at 86, page 86, because it's another example of the sort of unsupported or entirely partial conclusions that the witness seeks to draw. On page 86, we have the Convoy of Joy. What do we see at line 5? "The refugees then spontaneously attacked and took over the convoy, killing several of the drivers." Where is there, in his analysis of the material, any reference? And just as an example of the evidence going to suggest that, in fact, far from it being spontaneous, it was orchestrated. If you would look at footnote 461, you see, for example, Mark Thompson, a quoted article: "Thompson's credulity and uncritical reliance of Muslim sources is blatant, and his accuracy regarding the facts is contemptible." This is an astonishing document, as one can find, of course, in the opening paragraph at page 2, where the game is, in a sense, given away. At page 1, I beg your pardon, paragraph 2. What he says there is that: "It's one of the most basic rules of the historian, indeed of the police detective and others who seek to reconstruct past events" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to slow down, and perhaps you could come to a conclusion, Mr. Nice, given the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the point that is clear here is that he's simply seeking to do your job for you, but he's seeking to do it on testimony that isn't here, on interviews with anonymous informants who we aren't in any position to explore. He makes sweeping conclusions without any analysis of all the evidence, and he does all that without any relevant supporting expertise. The Chamber simply will not be assisted by this document, which will take some time to deal with in cross-examination, if he's called, but that shouldn't be a problem. It won't be assisted by this document. If this document should be admitted, as we say, then so should be the report of Dr. Cigar; not necessarily in all parts, because the Chamber expressed concerns about Dr. Cigar's expression or views on the final issues -- well, it wasn't actually the final issues, because the final issues here are the crimes. But as we suggested at the time, it would always be possible for the Chamber, in Dr. Cigar's report, to say, "Well, thus far, but not the next paragraph." But it would be quite wrong, quite unfair, to take this evidence, particularly given the way this has been prepared, and to exclude the evidence of a real expert, a Balkan expert and an analyst who, much more than Schrader, sources every conclusion he reaches by accessible material of one kind or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not have very much to add to what we've presented in our fairly short response. And I apologise for the shortness of it, but we only had overnight to prepare it. Our response sets out our position. We take the view that we have the right to present relevant expert testimony. Obviously, it's for the Trial Chamber to decide whether the testimony is relevant and helpful. We think that the testimony is relevant and it is helpful. The expert is a real expert, as we have outlined. He is a military historian, but he has extensive practical experience teaching on a wide variety of military subjects. He's an instructor, as we've outlined, in the Department of Unified and Combined Operations of the United States Army Command and General Staff College. He was the first acting director of the Combat Studies Institute in Fort Leavenworth. He has been a curriculum director for the NATO Defence College in Rome. So his experience goes beyond merely the experience of the American military, but he does have extensive military experience, having spent 23 years in the United States Army. He's extensively published. And just in conclusion, one comment that we made in our papers and I would like to draw to the Court's attention is this: In a war crimes case, it's hard to imagine testimony that would be more relevant and helpful than that of a military expert, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. We've had a variety of opinions offered in this case over the course of the last 15 months, Your Honours, as you know, and, in the Prosecution's case, a wide variety of military opinions offered by military people, microcosmic military opinions with the exception of Mr. Elford, who gave some very broad-ranging testimony. We think that we have the right to present an alternative view, the Defence's view, of what happened in the combat operations that took place in the Lasva, Lepenica, and other valleys in Central Bosnia from 1992 to 1994. Dr. Schrader does exactly that, and we think his opinion would be helpful to the Court. I don't have anything to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, while you are on your feet, I have several questions to ask you about this report which I have just glanced through. Was it compiled expressly for this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who ordered it, who asked for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I did, in all candour, me and my colleague Turner Smith, the lead trial counsel for Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think it is quite natural that the Tribunal be kept abreast of all the aspects if it is to pronounce itself. Was he paid for this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Initially, he was. Circumstances, I'm sure, cannot have escaped the Court's attention recently, and he has not been paid for preparing the last one third to one half of this report. He has actually volunteered his services in that regard, since he has been working with us for some time. So we're very grateful to him for doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Has Mr. Schrader ever been in the field during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mean Central Bosnia, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Not during the conflict, but he has been in Central Bosnia after the conflict, performing on-the-field visits to battlefields and so forth so that he can inform himself of the terrain features, and lines of communication, and things of that sort that are necessary to present an informed opinion of military operations in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, so he went out into the field so as to prepare his report, that was part of the preparation of his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, if I might just add this it would be hard to imagine, at least it's hard to imagine for me, any military expert who purports to offer opinions of any utility who isn't familiar with, so to speak, the lay of the land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Earlier in this trial, the Chamber had to deal with the report of an expert, Dr. Cigar who was to be called by the Prosecution. To this, the Defence objected essentially on the grounds that what Dr. Cigar was doing, although it was an extensive report, was giving evidence on the ultimate issue in the case, which it was a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine, and the Trial Chamber upheld those submissions. We now have before us the report of Dr. Schrader and the Prosecution, this time, make the same objection. We have had the opportunity of reading the report. We have considered the arguments, written and oral put forward by the parties, and we have come to the conclusion that this report should not be admitted for the same reasons as we excluded the report of Dr. Cigar. Essentially, this report purports to deal with the ultimate issues in the case. In this case, the ultimate issue is whether crimes were committed throughout Central Bosnia, who was responsible for the attacks on the various villages, for instance, was the village of Ahmici a justified target, was it defended or was it pure and simple a massacre. Now, those are issues which are very much matters which the Trial Chamber has to decide. In relation to the other villages, those near Kiseljak, for instance, similar arguments have to be decided. Finally, the village of Stupni Do, in which many people were killed, is a matter in which the Trial Chamber has to consider and to determine how it came about that these deaths occurred. Dr. Schrader is, in our view, an advocate and not an expert. He was entitled to be paid, of course, for his report but, nonetheless, we have to look at it and ask ourselves: Is it the report of an independent expert which will assist us in a relevant way? We've come to the conclusion that it's not relevant. It's not helpful because what it simply does is to set out the Defence case. And that is a matter not for an expert, but for the lawyers in the case. It's a matter for counsel to set the case to make their submissions which is what this report is essentially doing. A minor objection is that it relies in part on what would be hearsay from witnesses who are not apparently going to give evidence referred to by pseudonyms in some cases to whom the expert spoke with apparently during his visit to Central Bosnia. The matters can be illustrated fairly shortly, pages 35 to 55, for instance, are, in our judgement, essentially advocacy dressed up as military expertise using the materials in the case, the reporter doing that and then subbing them to argument. For instance, the treatment of the village of Ahmici refers at page 53 as it being a legitimate military target for a spoiling attack. Precisely, as I said, the issue to which we have to determine. That is, to give a brief indication of the tone of the report, that may be the way that Ahmici may be dealt with. The way that Ahmici is dealt with may be contrasted with the description of the ambush of Mr. Totic and the killing of his body guards, they are described as being brutally killed and Totic himself disappearing without a trace. On the other hand, that strong language may be contrasted by the language about Ahmici. That is, of course, a small point, but the matter may also be illustrated by the conclusion at pages 102 and 103 which I have to say, speaking for myself, reads like a sustained advocacy and not the independent report of an expert. Therefore, because it deals with the ultimate issues which the Trial Chamber has to determine. Because it is argument rather than expertise, and because the Trial Chamber finds the report relevant and not -- irrelevant, I should say, and not helpful, it will be excluded. The next matters with which we have to deal and I hope we can do so as rapidly as possible are the affidavits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let me get the papers together. In this connection, we have the affidavits in relation to Mr. Zoran Maric's evidence; Petrovic, Jovic, Bilanovic, Stipac and Hodzic and we have a table setting out the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I -- may I speak to the table and do so very briefly. I note the response of the Defence to our document. I don't think that needs any further observation unless the Chamber requires it of us. Before I come to today's table, may I remind the Chamber as we are not sitting next week. Theoretically, the seven day rule would be offended by later consideration of any affidavits whose power is spent. In respect of witnesses already served, may be in accordance the practice we've developed over the last two sessions; deal at a convenient time in the next sitting week or possibly the week after with affidavits that will fall for consideration having whatever extensions are necessary by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have three affidavits, Mr. Pervan, Ukic and Galuza.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They may not be spent yet in the sense that they may be in support of others to come and; I see Mr. Sayers nods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll extend the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've tabulated these witnesses in a different order than that read out by Your Honour, but I'm not going to make particular argument save in respect of two witnesses. As far as our basic and primary position is one of objection, but I move on. Nothing about Hodzic in particular. We've identified for the Chamber's consideration where matters are corroborative in form and where they're not. We have no particular observations to make in relation to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow that affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stipac, we do object to. An absolutely essential witness, and I have in mind the observation made by His Honour Judge Robinson. Also this is a person who witness Cicak said he was fitting into the category of those who would be a mastermind of the attack at the time. If one looks in what he seeks to say , he goes to some pretty central issues, and casting our eyes down the page on the second sheet number three, in particular, number five, I suppose, critically -- critically number six which is a matter in dispute and so on. So that he's a central witness and arguably somebody who was deeply involved in these matters on his own account and it must be highly unpalatable to have as affidavit witnesses those who may have other reasons to absent themselves from the Chamber. And the Chamber will have in mind, in that respect, one point that I draw from the Defence response to our position on affidavits where they seek to say that one of the affidavit witnesses eventually called before this Tribunal, Mario Santic was not moved in relation to central facts. Well, there's a great deal of potential argument for that particular witness, and very many points favorable to the Prosecution, but critically the Chamber will remember that Mr. Scott put to him, although he denied it, it may become the subject of later evidence, Mr. Scott put to him that he was in Ahmici and committing the attack at the material time. And it would have been quite unacceptable, the Chamber may think, for somebody with whom such issues could properly be ventilated to have come in which bay of affidavit and similar conditions apply to Mr. Stipac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, would you like to respond on Mr. Stipac?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Anto Stipac is 73 years old and in poor health, and that was one of the factors which led us to choose to put testimony by way of affidavit as opposed to calling him as yet another Busovaca witness in person. In our view, he covers almost precisely the same territory as Zoran Maric. He talks about interethnic relations in Busovaca before the war he talks about the Kaonik incident of May 9th. We've heard witness after witness testify live about that. He talks about the municipal HVO administration and the gradual restoration of order after the Kaonik incident. Again, witness after witness has testified about that. He does give some information about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He does give some information about the incident at the Kacuni checkpoint on the 20th and 21st and asserts that only Mr. Kostroman was involved in that incident, but the Court has heard again witness after witness about that. In connection with Mr. Cicak, he gives some evidence about Mr. Cicak not being a stable character, but Zoran Maric testified that Mr. Cicak had even shown him the certificate of mental incapacity that led to his early retirement, thus eliminating any privacy concerns that may have previously been articulated before that concern. But also, Mr. Maric related to Mr. Cicak that had he psychiatric problems and had difficulty controlling himself. But the testimony of Mr. Stipac in his affidavit on that is more general than the specific testimony that Mr. Maric gave on that point. He also gives general evidence about Mr. Kordic which the Court has heard about time and again, and the absence of any policy of persecution; exactly the same thing. So for those reasons, he doesn't offer anything, really significant in terms of specific factual testimony that has not already been the subject of extensive testimony before the Court and through Mr. Maric. He's not opining on issues of centrality, to use one of the Bench's member's words. So that's our position with respect to Mr. Stipac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we -- I think this is a witness who should be cross-examined. However, given his age, it may well be that he is a candidate for a video conference. I don't know what the state of play is about video witnesses, but he would seem to be an obvious witness who, given his age, should give evidence by way of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We will certainly consider that and with respect to video conference. I think that there are actually three individuals, perhaps four, at this point, who may have to testify by way of video conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're dealing with that, perhaps you can now be thinking about making arrangements for that to be done because it will require prior notice, clearly, to the Registry and arrangements to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President and I have that in mind and we hope to submit an application on the first day of the next session, June 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right, otherwise communicated through the usually channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: That means that you are not going to -- he is not going to testify in chief, this will be sufficient for you as testimony in chief or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If he testifies by videolink conference or if we can -- if his health permits, if we can get him here live, my approach would be pretty much the same approach that we've used with respect to the other affidavit witnesses, and to take about three minutes in direct just to have him confirm the accuracy of everything in his affidavit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that the Prosecutor, I believe, in the case of such a witness, the Prosecution should focus on elements which can be of relevance because this kind of cross-examination, I think, should only take a reasonable period of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nikica Petrovic is the last one on our list. This is the last of the witnesses that we are going to raise specific points of objection. I will draw the Chamber's attention to the couple of points in other witnesses for its exercise in discretion and judgement, but Nikica Petrovic has three really quite distinct grounds for objection. First, as the table reveals, there's a number of matters offered in his evidence which simply haven't been raised in the evidence of Maric, unless we are wrong in our analysis; two, three, four and five, and so on. The Chamber will note that there is a contrast, this is number 17 in the Maric evidence where what Witness DH said about being looked after by Dario Kordic appears to have been in complete contrast which is what is offered in the affidavit. Second point, Witness J told the Chamber that Petrovic was the only one who could grant permission for the leaving or not leaving of Busovaca. In light of the overall case concerning Busovaca, that's an important position for someone to have occupied and makes him a witness, who on that additional topic would be of great value to the Chamber. Third, not revealed on the document but something I must draw to the Chamber's attention, is this: The Chamber will recall that our policy in relation to witnesses was to use every means of compulsion to get them here or to get their evidence before the Chamber in one of the ways permitted by the Rules. I think we were almost the first case to use the extensive methods of compulsion available to the Chamber, and there is only one witness in respect of whom those methods of compulsion were ultimately entirely a failure, a woman called Enisa Begovic, and she having given a statement significant indeed, in its content, and apparently willing to give evidence, then about faced and refused to give evidence. She offered as explanation to us directly that she was dissuaded from giving evidence and that she was dissuaded by the mayor. And the Chamber may recall I touched upon this in relation to an earlier mayor of Busovaca, and it appears to us quite clear that the mayor with whom a conversation the woman had must have been Petrovic. And it would, of course, be wholly unconscionable for a witness, who may have interfered with the proceedings of this Chamber, to be allowed to give evidence by affidavit when such matters may properly be ventilated with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the point made about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the point made about the lady that the Prosecution identified. Obviously we know nothing and we're not in a position to comment upon that. We had a choice, Your Honours, to bring a chief of police to the Trial Chamber so that you could hear from him what the circumstances were like in Busovaca in regard to the civilian police administration in 1992 and 1993, and we did bring that witness along. That was Witness DG. We see no reason at all to bring along yet another witness to say pretty much the same things as Witness DG said, and that's been our general approach with respect to affidavits. Why bring along two witnesses when one will do and there is an affidavit? Unless the Prosecution can show a specific factual point upon which cross-examination is necessary, ordinarily it's our position that the witness shouldn't be required to attend. Apparently the only basis upon which the Prosecution wants this witness to attend is to conduct yet another roving-commission attack into credibility, and I, for one, don't think that that's a sufficiently substantial reason to require someone to come to testify. I also have in mind this is an interesting exercise in some regards, because the Prosecution, in an earlier part of this case, took the position that as long as there's some evidence on some particular point, then the witness statements which were verified and thus became affidavits, rambling in nature, very discursive, over a very wide period of time, that was sufficient just so long as they touched generally upon a point. And also there was one of those affidavits that specifically mentioned Mr. Kordic, and the affiant was not required to come in to testify, be subjected to cross-examination, notwithstanding contemporaneous objection by Mr. Kordic. That's as may be, though. But just generally speaking with respect to Mr. Petrovic, he really only offers evidence on four things; the Kaonik barracks incident, about which the Court has heard a lot of evidence; the increased crime rate in Busovaca as a result of a variety of causes, not the least of which was the huge influx of refugees from various other areas; he gives evidence again about Mr. Kostroman being at the Kacuni checkpoint and the only person who was apprehended there, Mr. Kordic not being there; and he gives evidence on the lack of any power on the part of the accused in this case Mr. Kordic to issue orders to the civilian police, a topic about which Witness DG testified extensively. So the testimony there is purely corroborative. It's not central to any issue, as far as we can see, and we don't see any reason to require this individual to come to court to experience yet another roving-commission attack on credibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've considered this carefully. We've noticed that there are some matters of controversy. We also note what the Prosecution says about issues of credibility. However, that's not a reason, in our judgement, to bring the witness here, given the fairly tenuous nature of the allegations. In those circumstances, given the balancing exercise which we are performing between the need to expedite the trial and also the need of fairness to both sides, we will admit this affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the balance, I've already indicated that I'm not going to raise particular objections. That doesn't deal with, of course, the Court's exercise of its own discretion, and I said that I would draw your attention to one or two points. In Bilanovic, again you'll see 1 to 4 simply not raised in the evidence allegedly supported. The Chamber will see in all of these witnesses' statements, in reality, central issues are being referred to. Of course, by our not raising specific objections, we aren't in any sense acknowledging the accuracy of the affidavit. We're simply doing what we believe the Chamber wants by way of cooperating in the exercise of its discretion and in accordance with the judgement it's formed on its power under the affidavit rule. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit those affidavits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other matters, and very, very briefly. One. Having referred to Enisa Begovic, she is the only witness who maintained defiance of the Court's orders, and I think I may have said on an earlier occasion that at some stage a decision ought to made about whether any action should be taken; not for now, obviously, but I must remember to deal with it. Second. Now that Dr. Schrader is eliminated, the three days' sittings of the week after next will obviously not be fully occupied by the one other witness, Dr. Jankovic, who is to give evidence. No doubt the Defence will be turning their mind to that, but I should alert them and the Chamber to the fact that the witnesses for the following week can't be accelerated because of the 21-day rule, and in any event we've already made fairly advanced arrangements to be able to deal with them in that week by securing the assistance of our own experts for that period of time, whether here in The Hague or elsewhere. But we wouldn't be able to deal with those other experts early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The week of the 20th is abbreviated anyway. It's a three-day week. Mr. Sayers, you've got the evidence to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we will be able to fill the week with evidence, Your Honour. Our plan is to produce two fact witnesses to round out the national witness case, if I may use such a term. They are Zoran Buntic, and I would just like to alert the Court that he has written an outline of his testimony which is substantial. I'm not confident that we can persuade him to truncate it, but what I propose to do is just gloss over the material that has already been covered with Mr. Perkovic and to try to accelerate his testimony in that way. But I just want to alert the Court, just in the interests of full information, that there's going to be a fairly substantial summary that comes in for him. But we do not propose to go through it. It's just there to be read, if you wish, but we'll try to avoid duplicating the testimony of other witnesses. The second witness is Zulfo Robovic, and then the third witness will be Professor Jankovic, and as I've previously alerted the Court, I don't think that he will last particularly long, and that may require us to advance some of the other witnesses. I have in mind the objection of the Prosecution, and we will not violate Rule 94 bis. Obviously, we'll try to fill in the time with some of our residual fact witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should have said, of course, confidential witness 4 is by no means a witness who we are confident we can conclude today, because we're only sitting until whatever it is, half past 2.00, and there's a lot to be raised with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for ten minutes for the witness to be called in and also for the Court to be reconstituted. Judge Robinson and I will sit alone, of course, to finish this witness and finish the evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, since we've had a break, we'll sit now until 11.30, take quarter of an hour then sit until one o'clock, half an hour and then sit until three unless that's inconvenient to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you. Your Honour, I have just tendered through the usher and this is highly unusual for me, and I felt after yesterday afternoon that perhaps this was the best way for me to -- forgive me. Your Honour, I have been with the Court's regular counselling to move forward with some efficiency, reviewed my outline and my notes over the evening. I can assure the Court I have deleted a volume of material by simply X-ing it out of my notes. However, I must urge the Court, this is a witness -- an extremely high-level witness. This is Mr. Boban's elbow during the critical time of this case. He is perhaps one of the two or three most senior witnesses the Kordic Defence will call. I hope the Court will note, I don't mean to be unduly offensive towards the witness, but that the witness has not been entirely responsive to many of the Prosecution's questions and it has been somewhat slower than what it might otherwise have been. I must also inform the Court, You Honour, in all honesty, that given today's schedule I think it is highly unlikely that we can possibly finish both of these very important witnesses. These happen to be two extremely important witnesses, probably for both sides, and we cannot expect to finish them I have to submit, Your Honour, today. So, I can tell the Court-- THE INTERPRETER Do slow down please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You can see from the outline, Your Honour, on even the reduced outlines, the matters that have not been covered and the Court may wish to tell me at some point, if the Court wishes to, what it would not want to hear about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will do that, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Some matters, for instance, looking at this document two you could put very broadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Yes, I appreciate that. Thank you. May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, when we left off, we were talking about the role, or the title of colonel that was given to Mr. Kordic. Let me put to you, sir, that in fact to the extent this represented some particular point in time that the title 'colonel' was conveyed, sir, it was nothing more than confirming powers that Mr. Kordic had had for a long time, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with such a view because he did not have any military powers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's your position then, sir, that despite what you've told us yesterday afternoon and despite the fact that he used this title, you persist in your position that Mr. Kordic had no military authority; is that what you're telling this Court?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour in the interest of time -- well let me show one, I will cut out a number but if the usher could tender to the witness Exhibit 395.1. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me indicate to you, sir, as the Court and the courtroom orients itself to this document. Sir, there are a number of documents in the record on which either Mr. Kordic is addressed as colonel or which he signs documents or has documents issued in his name in which the title or rank of colonel is used. Exhibit 395.1 is simply one example, sir. This is a document dated the 26th of January 1993, an order by Milivoje Petkovic. Would you agree with me, sir, looking at this, that this is clearly a military order?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that. It says, "Military Secret Strictly Confidential" up here. This is a document I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you look down paragraphs one through seven and I'm going to have to -- the Court's indulgence, if I stray over the line to be offensive to the witness, I'm sure the Court will tell me. Mr. Vucina, I'm going to have to insist that we move forward quickly with your answers and they be responsive, please. If you look through paragraphs one through seven, would you agree with me, sir, this is a military order talking about the disposition of forces, set defensive action, and disposition of HVO units. Would you agree with me, sir, this is a military order; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "order" in the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, there's no need to take these points up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It results to argument. The Court can make its own mind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will move on, and there are a number of other exhibits which I have cut from my--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help with one thing, have you any evidence or exhibit referring to Mr. Kordic as colonel before December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, Your Honour, there was one document but there was some question as whether the date of a document was a mistake, to be perfectly honest. I think the Court may be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's my recollection of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So that would be my answer, Your Honour. If it turned out that date was for some reason -- the earlier date was correct, then my answer to the Court would be yes, there is that document; however, I think there is perhaps some shared view that the date is probably wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on. You can deal with 2A briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you will allow me just to finish on this issue because there is another point to Mr. Vucina's involvement here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just finish with this, sir. It's your position that in fact despite the rank, despite Mr. Boban's decision, despite whatever processes were taken which you say you were directly involved in making him a colonel, that he was not, in fact, a colonel. Let me suggest to you, sir, you were then involved in perpetrating a falsehood on UNPROFOR in the International Community weren't you? You were involved in holding Mr. Kordic out to UNPROFOR as something that he was not, according to you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assert on the basis of some of the experiences that were generally accepted and applied in the Second World War that that is what was done. And if that was a mistake, then I cannot deny it, but this was on the basis of traditions. They existed earlier on with regard to such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to cross-examine on that. I think it would take us a long time. We don't accept that position, that theory. There's absolutely no details about what these other alleged instances or practices were. We don't accept that but, in the interest of time, we'll move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Other than to say, sir, you said yesterday, to finish on this point, this was an important matter. It was not a trivial matter. You said it was a matter of high importance, that the work of this mixed military working group was of great importance. In dealing with the International Community on this point, sir, I put to you again you were involved in holding out Mr. Kordic as something that you say he, in fact, was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point has been made, Mr. Scott. You have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just indicate, Your Honour, in moving on, sir, in paragraph 16 of your statement, you stated that the Muslims, "Practically wiped out the Bosnian Croat enclaves in Central Bosnia." And, sir, let me put it to you very briefly that statement is simply not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be allowed to say -- because a serious term was used. I would like to have a Croat translation of this that I said. I doubt that I said "wiped out". "Wiped out" would have meant that they disappeared altogether, and that is not my style of expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well, we have the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I can only refer again to the language in the English translation is what I'm quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 18 in terms of communications and travel problems between Mostar and Central Bosnia, can you tell us what those were very briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm just -- if you want to refer to it-- referring to your own statement, the period is not indicated in your own statement. It's paragraph 18, you simply say, in about the third or fourth sentence, in paragraph 18, "The Presidency itself met infrequently because of communications and travel problems. Dario Kordic..." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for having reminded me. This was in the period when tensions grew into open conflicts, incidents and broader, wider war operations. On the other hand, there is a road going from the north to the south of the country, and in the area of Mostar, this was under the artillery and other strong weapons of the Bosnian Serbs and the JNA. On the other hand, it was difficult to travel along other roads because there were checkpoints; HVO checkpoints, BH army checkpoints. On the other hand, there were war operations too, so it was difficult to communicate. Either in the west or along the Neretva River Valley, these were the only communications that were there. To the west, in the area of Bugojno just before the town itself, the army of Republika Srpksa or rather of the Serb army and the JNA, they controlled the road leading from Bugojno to the western part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me just ask you it this way then: Is it your position, is it your testimony that there was a substantial period of time in which Central Bosnia was cut off from Mostar by both physical communication, that is transportation, and by telephone or wire or other communications? Was it your position that Central Bosnia was cut off?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as communications are concerned, yes, and also telephones and I don't know about other means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how long was -- did this period of cut-off continue. When was that and how long did it continue, please, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: This primarily related to the intensification from January onwards. That is to say the intensification of war operations in Fojnica, Central Bosnia in general, that is to say, the end of winter the beginning of spring. Throughout this area, throughout this longer period of time, things were made considerably more difficult. Without the services of the peace forces, I think that it would have been very difficult for anyone to move about including aid agencies without the peace keeping forces, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me then try to see if we have it right. Are you telling us, sir, that really this period in which Central Bosnia was cut off from Mostar continued -- started in January 1993 and continued through that year of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. It all depends on the intensity of operations, and that was not the same on every day, on every month, on every week. But for the most part, the answer is, yes, the way you had put it, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, sir, -- and tell me if I'm wrong -- Mr. Kordic did not go to Mostar, did not travel to Mostar, was not in Mostar with Mr. Boban at any time during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that moment I mean, resorting to the services of the International Community, that is, Herceg-Bosna and the implementation of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. And then before that, the peacekeeping forces offered their goods and services, and it is only with their assistance that one could communicate and that certain areas were made accessible, and you could move from one area to another that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you then, sir, based on what perhaps you said yesterday, if we can move more quickly, you remind that -- is it correct, then, that the only time that Mr. Kordic, to your recollection, was in Western Bosnia or Herzegovina, in Mostar in this instance, Grude perhaps, was in August 1993 when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna changed to the Croatian Republic? Is that the only time, sir, you're aware, in 1993, of Mr. Kordic being in either Mostar or Grude? Please, just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I cannot confirm, though, whether there was a meeting before that and by way of preparations. Possibly then, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At most, sir, allowing for your memory, two instances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, at a maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell me, sir, the other way? Can you tell the Court, please, how many times in 1993 was Mr. Boban, to your knowledge, in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as far as I know -- not a single time, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've indicated -- in paragraph 18, you say: "Kordic was not in the high-level decision-making group who Boban consulted." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 23, you say: "Boban never consulted with Dario Kordic in reference to military matters." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I still go by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling the Court -- taking the position that Mr. Kordic, during 1993, was cut off in Central Bosnia and essentially, if I can say it this way, was on his own?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rights and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get the answer. I don't know if the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Rights and responsibilities," said the witness.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within his rights and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- what do you mean, sir? Let me back up for a moment. Forgive me, Your Honour. I'll come back to your answer, but let me first stay with my current question. Is it your position that Mr. Kordic, then, was cut off in Central Bosnia and essentially left to fend for himself or act on his own during 1993? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I'm the only person who believes -- I don't think he was on his own. There were other people with him. But if you are referring to contacts, there were telephone contacts from time to time, and also there were these major communication difficulties. The position was such --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that these people who belonged to local communities and to various bodies in these local communities could certainly function as well. It was necessary to ensure the functioning of everyday life, even in the hardest of circumstances, that is to say, public utilities, et cetera, and certainly they passed decisions in keeping with their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off, sir. I'm going to cut you off. One point of clarification. You say, "I don't think he was on his own. There were other people with him." You mean there were other people with Mr. Kordic in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you understand was Kordic's position -- when he uses the title"Vice-President", what was he the vice-president of during 1993? In your view, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established, he was, for a given point of time, the vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, and I think that at one of the meetings he was elected one of the vice-presidents. I imagine that that title was used in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your view, sir, of what the title "Vice-President" meant? What position was that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: One should look into the regulations that defined this. I dare say, on the basis of my own experience, that this was rather in nominal terms. This was an important-sounding title, in nominal terms, but basically without any work in the organ concerned; that is to say, on the basis of regulations. So it only had weight in conjunction with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your position, sir, that this position has been sometimes described as essentially the deputy speaker of the legislature or parliament of Herceg-Bosna, a body which apparently almost never met? Now, is that your understanding of what "Vice-President" meant?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of what my understanding is, there was a regulation, a piece of legislation that governed this relationship, and that is the only important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me ask the witness to please be shown -- I've skipped over about ten exhibits, but if I could ask the witness to be shown Exhibit 345 and 346. If they could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you have that Exhibit 345 in front of you. This appears to be the appointment of someone as the chief of the defence office in Central Bosnia, to one of those offices, by someone named Anto Puljic, the chief of the Travnik Defence Administration. Sir, it appears to be signed by and approved by Dario Kordic as vice-president, in this instance, of the party. If we can take both documents at once, 346 is a similar appointment, both of them dated in January of 1993, of a different individual again approved by Mr. Kordic as vice-president. Can you please help us, sir? Given the way you've described Mr. Kordic's role, or power, or lack of power, why would he be required then to approve of the appointment of persons as various heads of defence offices in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what I have been shown, it says that this is only a proposal of nominations for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter if it's a proposal or not. The point which is being put to you, Mr. Vucina, which the Court would like your answer on, is: Why is Mr. Kordic signing as vice-president? Can you help us with that or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, in the lower part it says "in agreement", so this is a process of nomination, the HDZ committee, and then it is only him as vice-president. So this is a process of nomination. The HDZ was a legitimate party that won the confidence of voters at the plebiscite in 1990. And then there is a column here that says an agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just, for a moment, concentrate on the question, Mr. Vucina. Why is Mr. Kordic countersigning the proposal, the appointment, whatever you like, as vice-president? Can you help with that or not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can, Your Honour, very gladly. I shall. It is signed by the president of the municipal board from which this person comes from, and then the vice-president and also the secretary. That was the procedure, that was the procedure. This is the agreement that was sought according to procedure, and obviously that is the procedure that was involved. And it is signed by the chief of administration, obviously, Anto Puljic. He is the one who signed it and put a stamp there. And this also invokes the provisions of Article 14, et cetera, whatever it says. So in the procedure, this was necessary, and this was what was done in practice as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on and come back to it a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is cadre policy, what is the term or phrase "cadre," c-a-d-r-e policy, mean in your political experience?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to explain this because I was on the executive committee of the HDZ. In terms of procedure, this is the way it was; we had the right to propose two or more candidates in the nomination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, sir, what is cadre policy? Just tell us what the two words "cadre policy" mean. Is that about immigration policy? Is it about personnel policy? What is cadre policy? That's my only question to you right now.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure of proposing candidates for positions of representatives or other positions in temporary government organs according to the requirements that are put forth for positions in various bodies of this nature or others. So the requirements mean what the person's qualifications are for that position and also what his conduct was like, et cetera. So that is what the procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please tender to the witness and put on the ELMO Exhibit 631.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This, sir, is the record of a meeting on the 8th of April 1993 which the Court will be familiar with. I note in light of recent testimony, if you look at the make up of the steering committee, you will see the first person listed is Colonel Dario Kordic, the first attended by Colonel Dario Kordic. Let me direct your attention please to page -- I can only say in the English translation it is page 6 and if you could find, it's the section dealing with initiating activities of the HDZ for BiH, if that helps you, but it should be in the translation around the fourth or fifth or sixth page. If we could put the sixth page on the ELMO, Mr. Usher. The top of that page -- if you can move it down a bit, please. Do you not see here, sir, at this meeting there was a resolution, an action taken that, "The party has to take charge of personnel policy in the municipalities, the army, the police, and the senior authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," isn't that correct, sir? Wasn't that the policy of Mr. Boban and the policy throughout Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I please be told exactly what point Mr. Prosecutor is discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I will repeat my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't see this document with which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't see the document. Let's have a look and see what page is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the top of page six in the English translation, and I apologise, on my working copy, I don't have a translation in front of me. At the top of page six, it says "The party".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we know where it is in the Croatian so the witness can see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, Your Honour. Your Honour, I've marked and will hand the usher a copy for ease of pointing it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Will you please direct your attention to the translation that's been pointed out to you, or I should say, the original. My question to you sir: Is that not, in fact, a statement of the policy in Herceg-Bosna that the party essentially had control or veto power, whatever you want to call it, a personnel policy in all these matters including the army, police, and senior authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, no. I assume that that is why one of these conclusions was put in this way, because quite a few nominations went apart from that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me put to you, sir, and then we'll move on. It was exactly this policy and practice, at least in part, that explains why Mr. Kordic would approve of the appointment of various senior officials to the defence offices, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, we'll move on. Sir, in your position as the head of the office of the president, did you not issue a statement on the 20th of December 1992 citing that, "The will of the Croat nation, on the basis of which Mate Boban has the mandate to represent it at the highest level, has expressed in the political charter of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Croatian Democratic Community," that is, the political party, "adopted at the second general Bosnia-Herzegovina HDZ assembly held in Mostar on the 14th of December." It was your position, sir, that the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the constitution must implement the political will of the HDZ political party. Do you remember taking that position, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to precisely remind me of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me do a little bitter than that. If the witness could be shown Exhibit 326.2. I hope copies can be provided of it as well. Sir, this is a statement that was made, there is a reference in the format that is a little tricky in some respects, but if you'll look several centimetres down from the top of the page at the left you'll see "1600 GMT, 20 December 1992". The document then states that -- starts out, "Haina, the Croatian news agency cites a statement by the office of the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna issued in response to a news conference given by Alija Izetbegovic in Zagreb three days ago, and Izetbegovic replied in the affirmative when asked if Mate Boban has given up the concept of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna." When I referred to you earlier, the particular language I just quoted you a moment ago was in the next to the last paragraph on that page starting, "This will of the Croat nation." Do you recall, sir, issuing this statement on about the 20th of December 1992? --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honorable gentlemen, evidently my intervention is needed because it says the 20th of December, 1992, not September as I -- it was interpreted to me. Secondly, this is a text of a news agency. This is not an official press release, press communication of any party official. Thirdly, this is a comment on Mr. Boban's statement. Official positions of the Croat Democratic Union, may I remind you, and I suppose this Honorable Court has them, were presented in the declaration by the Croat Democratic Union before this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you. If you look toward the end of that paragraph that I directed you to, the next to the last paragraph, the next to last and final lines say, "Which is signed by Srecko Vucina, head of the office of the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now that's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please give me the authentic document with my signature, then I shall be happy to comment on it rather than how the -- a news agency transmit conveyed my message. It is their freedom of expression, freedom of media and freedom of every individual journalist how he will interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, tell us then how please -- why was your view -- on what basis it was your view that the government and the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be required to implement the political will of one particular Croat political party?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that struck in a plebiscite one trust of the Croat people in the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina held in 1990, and was the only legal and legitimate will of the Croat people. We would have liked others to be in, because it would have made work much easier but, unfortunately, those were the circumstances one could not shun the responsibility gained through the electoral results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that Mr. Boban repeatedly denied the legitimacy, the legality and the legitimacy of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. But had they denied it, he would not have delegated representatives of the Croat Democratic Union under those hard wartime conditions to become members of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as I remember, Mr. Akmadzic was a member of this government and a member of the HDZ. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have extensive dealings with Mr. Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what you mean by extensive; frequent, long? If that is what you mean, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Frequent then, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But he held this same view, he held the same view that the political will of the HDZ party was, in fact, the superior expression of the Bosnian Croat people and that, in fact, he was anxious to move in the direction of a confederation or annexation with Croatia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there is will is shown by the results of the elections. All the other qualifications or statements I now, since I am under oath, cannot confirm. More than that, I cannot agree with them. This is confirmed by all our official documents. I remind you all our official documents, I do not go into private and personal views of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I submit that you haven't answered the question, but we'll move on. Is it true, sir, that at a meeting --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, please don't interrupt. Mr. Scott, you must really bring this cross-examination to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Allow me a moment, Your Honour, to edit as I go, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, one of a final two questions on this particular point. Is it your position, then, do you agree that it was the position of the party, your political party the HDZ-BiH, that the policies of the party would be realised and were to be realised in collaboration with and in agreement with the HDZ party in Zagreb and in political orientation, the HDZ-BiH was part of -- I stress was part of the HDZ; is that true or not? You can simply answer, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not true that we are a part because they are different party bodies, different presidents, different presidencies, different central bodies so that we are not a part of that body because there are two different statutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 16 of your statement, you say -- you mention a cease-fire agreement between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban on the 18th of May of 1993. President Tudjman was actively involved in those negotiations at that same time, as the Court will recall from a volume of evidence. I ask you, sir, why did you not see fit to include that in your statement when you talk about Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban? Why didn't you also tell us about Mr. Tudjman's extensive role in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to thank you for this opportunity, sir. Will you please show this Honorable Court a document to see in what capacity, what capacity, what powers, Mr. Tudjman had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we'll move on, Your Honours. The Court will have that.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I beg you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my only question to you, my only penned question pending to you --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I beg you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, what is suggested is that Mr. Tudjman had an extensive role in the negotiations. Do you agree with that or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours, and he signed it as a witness. It was the international meeting in Medjugorje. It was not a secret meeting. And we were very grateful, because it led to the end of the hostilities, the signing of a ceasefire. All war crimes were condemned. All the crimes and misdeeds on all sides were condemned. To establish a commission, coordination, that was a crucial moment, absolutely, in the establishment of mutual confidence. That is a very important document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll move on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The only question was why you did not see fit to include that in the description of events, but we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to skip over what you have as 6A. Let me just say to the Court, in the interests of time, the witness has made broad statements of no ethnic cleansing, persecution, or discrimination against Muslims. Obviously, the Prosecution does not accept that at all. It would take us an extended period of time to go through the evidence on that. We simply don't accept it. I will not go into the Ahmici issue because of time, only because of time, Your Honour. Let me go to the question of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what knowledge and involvement Mr. Boban had in either the, if you will, planning events -- of planning and leading up to Stupni Do or in the events in the aftermath of Stupni Do? Could you please tell the Court about Mr. Boban's involvement in that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I feel the need -- you said wrongly in your statement that I said that it wasn't, and I did not say that. I again guarantee under oath that these are not my words. I said that there was not any measures or any thought, especially in any political body in which I participated, and I once again vouch for this position here. I condemn every misdeed, I condemn every crime, as I did before they happened or whenever they happened, just as I thank the Lord for this opportunity to, before this august tribunal, say that I, Srecko Vucina, state for history that I condemn every crime and every misdeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, you're here to give evidence, which means to answer the relevant questions which this Court asks of you. Now, with respect, you are not here to make speeches. Let us go back to the question you were asked. The question was this: Did Mr. Boban have any involvement in the events in Stupni Do or in their aftermath? Now, can you concentrate on that question and give us an answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall be happy to do so, and I shall be very brief. But allow me that the Prosecutor alleged in his statement that I had said something that I had not. I was not familiar with the fact that Mr. Boban participated in any preparations or anything else. Personally, I have no knowledge of that. Personally, I doubt that any qualification of that kind could hold water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, then let me ask you to look at Exhibit 1268.3, if that could be tendered and the usher could assist us. While that's being handed out, sir, isn't it true that your office was involved in issuing a statement on the 28th of October, 1993, just days after Stupni Do, in which you denied that HVO soldiers were involved in that event, in the killing of civilians in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before me I again have a text which a news agency transmitted, and I cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, what is the relevant part of this, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a report, Your Honour, and there are various references in here as to the fact -- well, let me just say again that the top of the document says: "Report claims HVO did not carry out Stupni Do massacre." It talks about an investigation that was allegedly done, that the military and civilian -- I'm looking at the first paragraph, Your Honour. "The military and civilian bodies of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise. -- "have inspected the situation and the events on the territory under the control of the HVO." It goes on a couple of lines below that: "HVO soldiers did not carry out the massacre in the village of Stupni Do, nor did an armed HVO formation enter the undefended village." It states: "The report of the Public Relations Department of the Office of the President of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna." You were the chief of staff or head of the Office of the President, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is outside the period when Mr. Vucina was the head of the office of President Boban, so this is two months after that. And besides, I see here that this statement was signed by Mr. Slobodan Lovrenovic, and that is a different gentleman who worked in Mr. Boban's office at that time. So at that time, Mr. Vucina did not work in that office, because he worked there until the foundation of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna in August 1993. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
