utterances.text: I also feel the need to say that the person who was the spokesman of the office did that, and everybody performed his duties. So it was Mr. Lovrenovic who was the spokesman, rather than myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, is there anything else you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I can just be clarified on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you worked, in fact, with Mr. Lovrenovic, and was he, as is reported here, the -- I'm looking at the last paragraph, Your Honour, on the bottom of the first page. Was he, in fact, the president's public relation advisor?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was in the beginning -- end of 1992 or beginning of 1993 when Mr. Lovrinovic arrived in Sarajevo, and he did that from time to time; press releases and public relations. And after that, I believe, yes, that he officially did that, and after I finished my work in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, sir, why a report like this, which I submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, and do you have information because of your continued high role -- you were the president of the executive committee, you continued to have very senior positions in the HDZ structure -- isn't it true, sir, that Mr. Boban reported to President Tudjman about what happened at Stupni Do? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is outside party bodies, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in a meeting with Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Boban, where it was suggested that some of the same people who carried out the crimes in Ahmici were also responsible for Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never at a meeting at which only Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Boban were present. On a couple of occasions, I was at such meetings, but those were plenary meetings involving 15, 20, or perhaps more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you travel with Mr. Boban to any meetings with Mr. -- excuse me, President Tudjman in the second half of 1993 in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were at a meeting -- I think it was at about that time , I wouldn't know the month , when a large number went to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll move on, Your Honour. I would put, Your Honour, if I'm allowed, additional questions to the witness about Ahmici as well, similarly, but -- and certain people involved there, but I won't because of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in concluding your cross-examination, let me suggest to you that contrary to the picture that you've attempted to paint of Mr. Kordic, isn't it the case, sir, Mr. Kordic was the number-one HDZ political official in Central Bosnia, and in fact he, if you will, personified the policy and the execution of that policy in Central Bosnia in 1993; didn't he, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In compliance with the provisions of the statute, he was unquestionably the highest-ranking individual in that part, and under the -- and he unquestionably made the greatest contribution on the basis of the duties he was charged with under the statute and under the peace agreement. That is my position, my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, he was Mate Boban's man in Central Bosnia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't quite agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll only refer very summarily to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A number of paragraphs in your statement, sir, we don't have time to deal with them in detail; paragraphs 19, 27, 28. You talk about various assignments that Mr. Boban or others -- others gave to Mr. Kordic; to sell the peace plan, to do difficult things, that he had a difficult sales job. My question to you, sir, is: If the HDZ apparatus had a job to do in Central Bosnia, Mr. Kordic was the man they went to; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part in which it said regarding the implementation of the commitments we had undertaken under any peace plan, for instance, when it came to nominations for province governors, then that was my duty as the chairman of the executive board, I mean the nomination of individuals for bodies, executive and legislative, which were at a high level both -- either in the executive or the legislative branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in fact in paragraph 27, you equated, you and others that you associated with in the HDZ, equated Mr. Kordic with President Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you? In your view, he was just as significant and at the same level as Mr. Izetbegovic, and I put to you, according to your own statement, sir, that it was embarrassing. You said it was offensive that Mr. Kordic came to the meetings and his equal, the person at the same level. Mr. Izetbegovic, did not come to some of the same meetings; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you think. But let me just compare it. It is like the president of the Republican Party meeting the president of the Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go to paragraph 27, sir, the latter part going over on page -- in the English translation, Your Honour, on page 10. You and others were upset, sir, because you didn't feel that Mr. Kordic was being treated the same as President Izetbegovic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As presidents of two parties whose duty it was to enforce the Washington Accord. I repeat, presidents of two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My final two questions, Your Honour. I appreciate very much the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that in 1992 and 1993, the entire focus -- the entire focus of the Bosnian Croat institutions was on defence, was on military matters; there was no other political life, for all practical purposes, no separate political realm; everything was defence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say none other. For instance, locally in some municipalities, municipal boards, within their rights and responsibilities, tried to make their life go on. Central bodies, after some --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you would look at paragraph 3 of your own statement and about two-thirds of the way down into the paragraph on the bottom of the first page of your statement --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- I will quote you, simply quote you: "Our whole focus at that time was on defending ourselves through the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, the HZ HB, the HVO, and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna institutions. Normal political life had to be postponed until after the Washington Agreement." That's your own statement, sir, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. But I should like to complement it with a sentence that during that time of war, the HDZ was not all that active so would you please read the sentence before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, the Court will just have to take that statement for itself on the basis of what we've covered whether the party was not, in fact, active during this period. Let me submit to you in closing Your Honours and to the witness. Sir, your statement is, in fact, correct in this instance, it was the entire focus. In Central Bosnia, sir, there was no other man, there was no other official, there was no other person more responsible for those matters and for the Defence and for military actions and the strategy of the Bosnian Croat people than Mr. Dario Kordic, was there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is a question to me, I will say I cannot agree with you and your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, but very short. Mr. Vucina, a great deal was said today about the HDZ. I have only one question, please. Will you tell Their Honours which political party of the Croat people, that is, Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the counterpart of the International Community in the conclusion of all peace agreements from so-called Cutilliero's plan to the Dayton Accord?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban signed Cutilliero's plan, Vance-Owen Plan and Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and after him, the Washington Agreement, it was Mr. Kresimir Zubak. The Dayton Accord was initialled by professor -- Dr. Jadranko Prlic, signed by Kresimir Zubak on behalf of the Croat people as the legal and legitimate representatives of the Croatian Democratic Union. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you answered to a question that, theoretically speaking, my colleague warns me that the last question was not interpreted to the end, that this part is missing about the HDZ, that witness, Vucina, mentioned but we can do it later, resolve it through our objections to the transcript. You spoke about the theoretical possibility that Mr. Mate Boban, as the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and commander in chief, could delegate some of his powers, some of his authority including the military ones to another individual; is that so? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So my question to you is as follows: Mr. Vucina, did you ever, during all the time that you were in the immediate vicinity of Mr. Boban hear him delegate any of the military authority to any other person including Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even when he was abroad, not even then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Incidentally, I also need to ask you, please do not hold it against me, perhaps it will sound strangely, but because of some words which were uttered in this Court a long time ago, will you tell us, please, when did Mr. Boban die or perhaps I should ask whether he died because of some rumours, but --

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it will be an anniversary shortly and we shall celebrate holy mass. I was on my summer holidays and I received the news. It was the 7th or 9th, I returned from the holidays, I attended the funeral at the holy mass and I do it every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I did not hear you say the year.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO VUCINA:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be the third anniversary, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, Your Honours, I do not have any further questions, too many subjects were broached, but I'm afraid that we shall -- we would spend too much time on that. Thank you very much. Thank you witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucina, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've asked for the witness to be kept out briefly. The same issues arose with confidential witness number three. The Chamber will recall my concerns on behalf of the OTP in relation to witness number three that when witnesses come in these circumstances, we cannot even know why they seek protection. The Chamber will recall that witness number three, when asked by me, gave an explanation what happened when asked the question -- which was unexceptionally revealed that he was frightened of no one, and eventually said, -- when asked why he had sought protection, in the form of a closed session, that if you're given the option of in the form of a closed session, you choose one or the other. We were under very understandable and proper pressure which we respected at all times to have as much of our case in public as possibly could be in public. The Chamber will recall that I undertook at the beginning to deal directly with every witness. I wasn't able, in the event, to do that personally to ensure that any request for protection was justified and, of course, always made available to the Defence. The Chamber will recall that two of at least of the witnesses came with the forecast of protection then gave evidence in open session. And for this witness, we can see no reason manifest from his summary or from anything we know about him that would justify him giving evidence in closed session and we must object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I do not have on hand the documents or the submissions which were made to us as to why this witness should be confidential; however, an application was made, and we ruled on it as a Trial Chamber allowing the witness to be treated as a confidential witness. So part -- I can see no reason to go back on that rule which was no doubt -- which was made for good reason. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm certain you'll agree with the Presiding Judge, and I wanted to say that, as a matter of principle, I don't think the procedure you've adopted is correct. Once the Chamber has made a ruling, that's the ruling. I think if you wish to challenge it, then you should do that elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not -- I understand what Your Honour says, but with respect, the point that has to be appreciated and underlined is that in these very particular circumstances, rulings are made ex parte. Whereas in relation to every other witness who seeks protection, the opposing party has a right to be heard, so that we are in no position to justify -- not "to justify". We are in no position to evaluate the ruling that's been made, save, of course, when we ask the witness questions about it. I'm certainly not going to go appeal, on an interlocutory basis or probably at all, such decisions. But it's my duty to draw to the Chamber's attention that the decision that's been made was made ex parte and is one that we cannot at the moment, on the sight of the documents available to us -- if I say "understand", you'll think I'm being offending. I don't mean that. We can't understand, simply from the documents available to us, why that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think that's to be taken up here. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Have the witness and a pseudonym, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness will be DK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, Your Honour, let me just alert the Trial Chamber to the fact that he will not be available when the Court sits again on the week of the 20th, and he tells us he's not going to be available until September, which is one of the reasons we wanted to get his testimony completed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see how we get on with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 3.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
